RagShortTexts: Poison fears concern kitchens, servers and trust, and rumours easily become accusations.
Tasting or watching silver cannot ensure safety, nor does illness alone prove poisoning.

Variants.Content:
A host with enemies worries who entered the kitchen, brought a wine jar or served a dish. Many people handle purchase, storage and cooking; spoiled leftovers, dirty vessels and mistaken ingredients also cause illness, though onlookers may immediately suspect a plot. Trusted duties and known vessels make later inquiries easier without removing every risk.

Some trust tasting or a change in silver as reassurance, but foods, utensils and onset times differ, and one uneventful taste does not prove a table safe. A suddenly ill guest needs care, drink and experienced help while the host asks who ate what. Threatening servants into admissions turns fear and guesses into statements and damages household ties.
Lords need care for patients and clear accounts from kitchen workers. Punishing guesses can silence people who actually know purchases and handovers.
Guards respond to poison alarms without rash violence or blocking care. Ill travelers need accounts of food, water and companions rather than an immediate scapegoat.
Kitchen workers’ livelihoods suffer when guests fall ill. Clear recollection of supplies and handovers explains events better than echoing a patron’s suspicion.
